name: Christian reconstructionism
summary: Christian reconstructionism is a Calvinist theonomic movement, founded by R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen and Gary North, which holds that Old Testament civil law remains binding and that society should be rebuilt under Christ's lordship in every sphere. It expects gradual, postmillennial Christian dominion through regeneration, family, Christian schooling and church rather than revolution, favors a decentralized limited state and private property, and opposes statism and democracy as a source of authority.
scope: The mainstream theonomic movement as set out in Rushdoony's Institutes of Biblical Law, Bahnsen's Theonomy in Christian Ethics and North's economic writings, as described in Chalcedon material, John Frame's review and Wikipedia. It excludes later dissenters such as Joel McDurmon's retreat from death penalties, and non-theonomic Christian right politics.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Rushdoony wanted health, education and charity returned to private and covenantal hands, so a state-guaranteed system is rejected as statism.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Reconstructionists are described as favouring libertarian economics, yet Rushdoony called laissez-faire godless, so the strand's view is contested.

public-ownership.rationale: Rushdoony attacked statism and held that eminent domain belongs to God alone, so state ownership of major industries is opposed.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Rushdoony opposed property taxes and expropriation beyond the tithe, so higher punitive taxes on the wealthy are rejected.

property-fundamental.rationale: Frame reports Rushdoony holding eminent domain belongs to God alone and criticizing humanists who define property out of existence.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare is to be provided through church, family and covenantal institutions rather than the state, so state welfare should be ended.

strong-leader.rationale: Rushdoony preferred a republic with separated powers and decentralization, not a leader bypassing gridlock.

state-harmful.rationale: Rushdoony called for radical decentralization and a limited state, but accepted civil government (courts, defense) as ordained by God, so not anarchist.

empower-police-military.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.

reviewHistory.rationale: Rushdoony wanted a society nearly without prisons and criticized war taking precedence over other activities, though he favored strong enforcement of law.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Theonomy treats sexual offenses such as adultery and homosexuality as capital crimes in a Christian order, so legal prostitution is rejected.

decide-locally.rationale: Rushdoony explicitly called for radical decentralization of government and society.

rehabilitation.rationale: Frame reports Rushdoony wanted restitution and execution of serious offenders and a society without prisons, rejecting rehabilitation-centered incarceration.

traditional-family.rationale: Rushdoony held the family is the basic institution of society with a biblically established authority structure.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Male homosexuality is treated as a capital crime in Rushdoony and theonomists, so legal same-sex marriage is firmly rejected.

abortion-legal.rationale: Abortion appears as a repeated concern in Rushdoony's Institutes and, as murder under biblical law, is opposed; Frame does not state it, hence medium.

more-religion-public.rationale: The movement's aim is to bring every area of life into captivity to Christ and reconstruct society under Christ's lordship.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Rushdoony held fixed biblical roles and male-female distinctions, including that men doing woman's work is wrong.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Rushdoony admired a Christian 19th-century America, but he emphasized Christian faith over nationality, so only mild agreement.

gradual-change.rationale: Rushdoony opposed violent revolution and favored gradual regeneration beginning with individuals and families, though not deference to existing secular institutions.

nation-first.rationale: Not a defined position; loyalty is to God's law and kingdom more than nation, but also opposes global governance.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Reconstructionists hold that regeneration through God's law, not technology, solves society's problems.

revolution-justified.rationale: Rushdoony opposed participation in revolution and favored gradual regeneration, though Rahab-type wartime ethics are defended.

experts-over-public.rationale: Rushdoony rejected claims of neutral expertise and statist rule; authority rests in God's law and families.

central-planning.rationale: Rushdoony attacked statism as a drain on the economy and rejected state control of economic life.

socialized-markets.rationale: Rushdoony rejected public ownership as statism; worker-owned markets are not endorsed, but voluntary ownership is permitted.

land-value-tax.rationale: Rushdoony opposed property taxes, which a land value tax would resemble.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Rushdoony's biblical law stresses family inheritance, and no taxation beyond the tithe is allowed.

basic-income.rationale: Welfare is a covenantal, not state, duty and the state may not expropriate beyond the tithe.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Statism is rejected and the state is only one limited sphere of authority.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Rushdoony stressed family property and inheritance and a family-centered society, but never made wide distribution a policy goal.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Biblical economics involves private property, contract, wages and the tithe; abolition of money is foreign to it.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognized bodies setting wages are statism, contrary to decentralized, voluntary institutions.

one-party-rule.rationale: Rushdoony saw Christ as the supreme authority, civil government as limited, and the state as one institution among several.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Rushdoony preferred a republic with separated powers; hereditary monarchy is not endorsed, though kings appear in the Bible.

democracy-best.rationale: Rushdoony called Christianity radically anti-democratic and preferred a republic restraining majority rule under God's law.

workers-councils.rationale: Power rests in God's law and in families, church and limited civil government, not in workers' councils.

natural-rulers.rationale: Authority comes from God's law, not natural aptitude; mixed with a view that regenerate Christians should lead.

political-violence-never.rationale: Rushdoony opposed revolution but defended capital punishment and wartime ethics, so violence is not absolutely excluded.

war-builds-character.rationale: Rushdoony held war should not take precedence over other human activity and that production precedes politics.

separate-church-state.rationale: Reconstructionists distinguish spheres of authority yet reject neutral secular government and want civil law under God's law, so strict separation is rejected.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Theonomy holds Old Testament civil law remains normative and civil government must enforce it.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Rushdoony included courts of arbitration among non-statist institutions but kept criminal justice and defense for civil government.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The covenantal community is defined by faith rather than ethnicity; Reconstructionism formally rejects racialism.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Rushdoony saw history as governed by God's providence and the conflict of faiths, not class.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Biblical law gives equality before the law, not outcomes, and rejects state redistribution.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Obligation to God's law is primary, but Rushdoony also defended property rights strongly.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Creation is under human dominion mandate, with value derived from God, not intrinsic apart from humans.

limit-population.rationale: Dominion mandate and pro-family stance oppose population control; not directly stated in opened sources.

restore-past-order.rationale: Rushdoony looked to biblical law and an earlier Christian America, but combined with a forward-looking postmillennial hope.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Reconstructionists hold that God's law is the fixed standard, not results.

direct-action.rationale: No simple political answer; change through education, family and church rather than elections or direct action.

means-match-ends.rationale: Rushdoony stressed rebuilding from family and community upward, reflecting the society desired, but not as explicit principle.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Dominion over creation mandates culture-building, not a return to foraging.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Biblical economics includes distinct callings and roles; Rushdoony defended distinct work roles.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Private property and the tithe govern provision; need-based distribution by the state is statism.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Profit is legitimate under biblical property law; the exploitation thesis is a Marxist premise.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Rushdoony rejected revolution and statism and held the state limited under God's law.

collective-farming.rationale: Biblical law protects family land and inheritance, opposing collectivized farming.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Rushdoony attributed war and decay to statism and humanism, not capitalism.

taxation-theft.rationale: Rushdoony opposed property taxes and taxes beyond the tithe, but accepted limited civil government funded under biblical law, so not simply theft.

harm-principle.rationale: Theonomy punishes offenses defined by biblical law, such as blasphemy and adultery, beyond harm to others.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Rushdoony stressed the family and covenant institutions as authority-bearing spheres, so rights are not purely individual.

state-as-business.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value turns on whether citizens are customers who can leave, and the statement now asks only whether government should be run on business principles.

reviewHistory.rationale: Rushdoony resisted treating the state as the economic actor; the state's role is justice, not customer service.

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value turns on whether citizens are customers who can leave, and the statement now asks only whether government should be run on business principles.

positive-liberty.rationale: Rushdoony held that state provision of material means is statism, with welfare via covenantal institutions.

media-academia-power.rationale: Rushdoony was a sharp critic of secular humanist education and the humanist establishment, which he saw as holding cultural power.

organic-representation.rationale: Rushdoony saw government beginning with persons and families and wanted decentralized covenant institutions, resembling organic representation.

total-state.rationale: Rushdoony opposed statism, where the state controls all areas of life, and objected to calling the state the government.

national-rebirth.rationale: Rushdoony diagnosed Western decay and urged regeneration, but in terms of Christian faith rather than nation.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority rests on covenant under God's law rather than feudal personal oaths.

bound-labor.rationale: Frame reports Rushdoony forbade new-covenant believers from entering slavery.

universal-morality.rationale: God's law is binding on all men and nations, though it is revealed in Scripture more than discoverable by reason alone.

single-common-good.rationale: Reconstructionists reject neutral pluralism and seek a godly order, but through revelation, not reason alone, so only partial fit.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Rushdoony saw the family and voluntary institutions, not democratic voting, as the basis of authority.

school-vouchers.rationale: Rushdoony wanted Christian schools and homeschooling independent of the state, rejecting public funding and control.

economic-freedom.rationale: Reconstructionists favor libertarian economics, while Rushdoony held that freedom rests on Christian self-government more than economics.

rule-by-example.rationale: Reconstructionists emphasize codified biblical law and penalties, not example.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Reconstructionism holds Scripture is the supreme authority and that no knowledge is neutral or autonomous.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare is by church and family for covenant members, and state welfare is rejected overall.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Biblical economics rejects dependency, and charity through covenant institutions is conditioned on work.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Rushdoony held that men and women have distinct biblical roles, such as the head covering as submission and men doing woman's work being wrong.

ban-interest.rationale: Rushdoony's treatment of usury is unclear in my sources; biblical law forbids interest on loans to the poor only, so a general ban is not supported.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Reconstructionism holds God's law applies equally to all peoples; legal racial segregation is not a biblical-law position.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Rushdoony saw the state as a limited institution under God, and class-instrument analysis as Marxist.

national-mission.rationale: American exceptionalism is a theme of some, but Rushdoony spoke of Christ's kingdom triumphing everywhere, not national mission.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Biblical family authority structure is affirmed, not seen as unjust advantage over women.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Rushdoony criticized statist rulers as humanist, but not as a general populism.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Civil government is limited to criminal justice, courts and defense, but also enforces biblical law including religious offenses, so only partial.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Reconstructionists define covenant by faith, and the sources show no racial doctrine.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: All people are under the same God's law, though non-Christians are excluded from full citizenship by some writers.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The theonomic view punishes promoting false religions, but not preventing conversion to Christianity; ambiguous.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Dominion mandate allows use of animals.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Rushdoony opposed state schools as humanist and wanted Christian education, though he did not want the state to run religious instruction.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Authority comes from God, and Rushdoony disparaged democratic legitimacy.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Theonomy legitimates state force against offenders but opposes aggression by the state beyond that.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Rushdoony opposed state censorship in general, though blasphemy is punishable.

separated-powers.rationale: Rushdoony preferred a republic with separated powers to restrain majority rule.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Care of the poor is a duty via the covenant community, though not a state priority.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Rushdoony regarded children as blessing; poverty comes from sin and statism.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Not a doctrine; cohesion comes from shared Christian faith and law, which is mildly in support.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Rushdoony rejected democratic rule; lottery runs against biblical legal order.

party-controls-media.rationale: Rushdoony opposed totalitarian statism over all areas of life, including media.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Opposed to centralization and humanist world government.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Reformed and Presbyterian polity of elders, and Rushdoony's elders led enterprises, not bishops.

clerical-rule.rationale: Rushdoony rejected the church acting as a state; civil government is distinct from church, though under God's law.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Blasphemy is punishable, but broad censorship of art is not described in the sources.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Rushdoony was a sharp critic of secular education and its elites.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Rushdoony held that Christian faith and biblical law are the standard, so cultures are not equal.

death-penalty.rationale: Rushdoony and theonomists defend capital punishment for murder and many other crimes.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Rushdoony opposed state education and favored Christian and home schooling.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Rushdoony wanted creationism taught in Christian schools but opposed state schooling altogether, so the answer on public-school curricula is split.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Rushdoony served as expert witness in religious liberty cases, though for Christians chiefly.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Conformity to biblical norms is encouraged.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Biblical law treats debts as binding, though debt release is also found in Scripture.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Charity is covenantal, not state aid.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Property is held under God's law, but Rushdoony opposed defining property out of existence, so rejects the conditional justification.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The Soviet system is condemned as statist and humanist, but the specific state-capitalist label is a Marxist dispute with no Reconstructionist stance.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Rushdoony held the church and family are distinct spheres, with the state limited.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Rushdoony rejected treating the state as divine and held that civil government is not a mediator of God.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Rushdoony opposed state taxation beyond the tithe, favoring minimal and flat taxes.

character-from-environment.rationale: Character is formed by regeneration and sin nature, though upbringing matters in the covenant family.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Theonomy binds every ruler, the civil magistrate included, to God's law, so a ruler above law is rejected.

space-expansion.rationale: Dominion over creation is a mandate, but space is never discussed in the sources.

leader-cult.rationale: Honoring a leader with statues would be idolatry in a movement that treats the state as limited and under God.

land-redistribution.rationale: Rushdoony rejected state expropriation beyond the tithe and held eminent domain belongs to God alone.

women-must-cover.rationale: Rushdoony saw the head covering as a sign of submission in 1 Corinthians but did not call for legal enforcement in the review.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Rushdoony held history is driven by God's providence and religious presuppositions, not material conditions.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Rushdoony distrusted majority rule but wanted law bound by God, not courts bound by majority.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Distinct biblical roles for men and women oppose mandated parity.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Rushdoony stressed teaching Christian history and presuppositions, though the statement concerns nation or civilization.

patriotic-education.rationale: Rushdoony wanted Christian education and criticized state schooling; patriotism is not the aim.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Rushdoony saw Western economics in decay, but not a collapse thesis.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Rushdoony saw the US Constitution as designed to protect religion and states' rights.

elective-rulers.rationale: Rushdoony preferred a republic with representatives, but hostile to democracy as a principle; mixed.

parliament-supreme.rationale: God's law is supreme over any legislature.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animals are creatures under human dominion; Scripture condemns cruelty, but not explicit in sources.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Dominion mandate allows use of animals.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Charity as covenant duty of the wealthy is biblical, though framed as family and church responsibility.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The movement aims to reconstruct every area of life, so withdrawal is rejected.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency theory is not part of the movement.

party-own-road.rationale: A communist-party strategy question with no Reconstructionist stance; opposed to communism altogether.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Aid belongs to covenant institutions, not states.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Rushdoony opposed totalitarian statism of any kind.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Rushdoony wrote a revisionist view of the Civil War and defended states' rights; unverified by my sources.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Rushdoony admired the historic Christian American order.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The army is not a political arbiter; Rushdoony limited the state.

paid-care-work.rationale: Family work is a God-given duty, not state-paid labour.

filial-duty.rationale: Frame reports Rushdoony stressing children's obedience and family authority.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Rushdoony applied biblical divorce law, with limited grounds, so divorce without fault is rejected.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Biblical law protects family land and inheritance; state ownership is rejected.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Law is based on equal biblical standards, not outcomes, and libertarian economics rejects it.

corporate-influence.rationale: Rushdoony criticized statism more than corporations.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: The family should be fruitful, but state subsidies are statist.

residents-only-property.rationale: Property rights oppose local limits on purchase.

job-guarantee.rationale: State employer of last resort is statism.

democratic-peace.rationale: Rushdoony distrusted democracy as a principle.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: God's law binds all and Rushdoony condemned revolution.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Not a doctrine of the movement.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Rushdoony set out a biblically defined marriage and divorce law, so removal of legal marriage is rejected.

informal-organisation.rationale: Anarchist movement structure is not part of the program, which works through church, family and school institutions.

religious-nation.rationale: The movement seeks a Christian society, but it also stresses voluntary regeneration over imposed national identity.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.

reviewHistory.rationale: Private property is basic in biblical law.

defeat-communism.rationale: Reconstructionists oppose communism as humanist statism; Rushdoony stressed battle of worldviews.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Rushdoony wanted services privately provided, not mixed with state.

religion-illusion.rationale: Christ's lordship over every sphere is the movement's core claim.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Libertarian economics yes, but Rushdoony rejected laissez-faire.

socialized-care.rationale: Rushdoony held that the family, not the state, bears care and education.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Rushdoony rejected both statism and laissez-faire, seeking biblical economics.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Rushdoony held male homosexuality is a capital crime, and theonomists prescribe criminal penalties.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Frame and Wikipedia report Rushdoony prescribing execution of blasphemers and punishment of false-religion promotion.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: An Islamic doctrine with no Reconstructionist stance.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Rulers who flout God's law are illegitimate in principle, but Rushdoony opposed revolution.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Rushdoony framed conflict as Christian versus humanist, not left-right.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist concept; Reconstructionists treat work as a calling under God, so it is rejected.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Rushdoony held that Christ's lordship covers the state and rejected popular sovereignty.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Rushdoony defended religious liberty, but for Christian practice.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Defense is a legitimate state function.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Dominion mandate and Rushdoony's role views oppose it.

reification.rationale: A Marxist concept with no place in Reconstructionist thought.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Reconstructionists insist on fixed, publicly given biblical law.

citizens-assembly.rationale: The movement opposes democracy as a source of authority and wants law drawn from Scripture, so assemblies of lot-chosen citizens deciding public questions are rejected.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Theonomy treats biblical law as binding and Rushdoony read almost all Old Testament civil law as literally normative, so modernizing reinterpretation of doctrine and law is rejected.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Theonomy treats Old Testament civil law as binding, including penalties for homosexual acts, so open service is rejected.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The movement wants society under Christ's lordship and Christian schooling, so a state promoting atheism is the opposite of its aim.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Theonomy requires a civil magistrate that enforces biblical penal sanctions, so police and prisons are kept in some form.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Rushdoony wanted health, education and charity returned to private hands, family and church.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Reformed theonomists hold that church offices of teaching and rule are reserved to men.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Theonomy retains Old Testament civil law with its capital penalties and defence of life and property, so a refusal to kill in self-defence is rejected.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Reconstructionism frames all spheres of life as under Christ's lordship and in conflict with humanism, so politics is a spiritual struggle.

culture-before-state.rationale: The movement expects change gradually through regeneration, family, church and Christian schooling before state action.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Scripture is the infallible standard that judges all, and Rushdoony defends biblical roles for women as Frame summarises, so the test is reversed.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Reconstructionists reject socialism as statism and take political authority to rest in God's law, not in a class, so worker power is no test of a just society.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Rushdoony wanted welfare, schooling and other services provided privately by family and church, not by the state, and favoured a minimal civil government.

municipal-property.rationale: They defend private property as a biblical right and reject collective ownership, whether by the community or the state.

person-over-state.rationale: Reconstructionists hold that God's law, not the individual, is the ultimate authority and that the state should be limited by it; this is not a view that the state exists to serve the person as such, though they oppose treating persons as means of the state.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Christ's lordship over every sphere of life, and religion as the basis of society, are central to the movement.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The movement grounds identity in covenant faith, not race, and its major figures rejected racial group politics as unbiblical.

free-public-college.rationale: Education is held to belong to parents and the church, and state schooling is rejected; tax-funded state colleges follow the same logic.

capital-controls.rationale: The movement favors private property, free markets and a minimal state (Gary North's economics), so state control of capital flows conflicts with it.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: The movement opposes the welfare state and statist redistribution, holding that charity belongs to family and church.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: North and others treat debt as a bondage the Bible warns against and want government kept small and limited in its spending.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The movement expects gradual change through regeneration, family and schooling, and rejects revolution, though it does want the current order eventually replaced.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The movement holds that biblical law supplies the one binding blueprint for society, economics included.

sacred-nation.rationale: Reconstructionists place covenant and God's law above the nation and treat sacralising the state or nation as idolatrous.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Biblical law is read as requiring that debts be repaid, and state-funded relief is statist redistribution.

religions-one-truth.rationale: The movement holds Christianity alone as true and binds society to Christ's lordship, rejecting religious pluralism.

farm-price-support.rationale: The movement favours free-market economics and a limited state, which excludes state price guarantees.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: The movement applies Old Testament restitution law to harm and favours private property, not administrative agencies.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Theonomy applies Old Testament penal law with its prescribed penalties instead of discretionary sentencing.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Theonomy holds that biblical law should govern the civil order, so one reading of Christianity, the Reformed theonomic one, should have legal precedence.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Reconstructionists oppose democracy as a source of authority, holding that legitimacy comes from God's law and not from electoral procedure.

premarital-sex.rationale: Rushdoony's Institutes of Biblical Law treat sex outside marriage as sin and, in strict theonomy, as a civil offence.

women-suffrage.rationale: Reconstructionists often favour household representation under male headship, which doubts an individual vote for women, but positions vary and the sources are thin.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: The movement defends biblical patriarchy and regards Christianity as the foundation of social order, so it rejects the claim.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Dedicated state agencies for gender equality conflict with the movement's opposition to statism and its view of family government.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Rushdoony's Institutes treat Scripture as the infallible, binding word of God, as Frame's review describes.

defend-planned-state.rationale: The movement opposes statism and regards a state-run economy as an idol, whoever rules it.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The theonomic penal system demands due process and witnesses under biblical law, so execution without trial is rejected.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: The movement defends private property under biblical law and opposes redistribution; Gary North's economics are explicitly pro-property.

self-ownership.rationale: Reconstructionists hold that man belongs to God and is not his own, so self-ownership as an autonomous right is rejected.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The movement wants welfare done by family and church not the state, so neither design is endorsed.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: The movement stresses decentralised covenantal institutions and opposes concentration of power in a state leader.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The movement wants civil government under biblical law, which is not neutral among religions, though it does not seek denominational parties.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Rushdoony's Institutes grounds divorce in biblical law under male headship and covers only limited biblical grounds.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Reconstructionist economics defends property gained honestly and rejects equality as the measure of justice.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: The movement opposes new state taxes and favours a minimal state financed by tithes.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Theonomy holds that law derives from God and human law that contradicts it lacks authority, so disobedience is a duty.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: The movement's economics follow free-market and Austrian ideas and oppose Marxism.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: The movement is strongly anti-communist and holds that statism is idolatry.

police-more-powers.rationale: Rushdoony wanted a society nearly without prisons and criticized war taking precedence over other activities, though he favored strong enforcement of law. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Welfare is to be provided through church, family and covenantal institutions rather than the state, so state welfare should be ended. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Christians have a duty to take dominion over every area of life, including government, education and the economy.
missingStatements.rationale: Rushdoony's dominion theme holds that nothing is exempt from Christ's rule and every area of life must be brought into captivity to him.

missingStatements.text: Education is the responsibility of parents and the church, not the state.
missingStatements.rationale: Rushdoony defended Christian schools and homeschooling against state control and wanted health, education and charity returned to private hands.
missingStatements.declined: Overlaps school-vouchers and no-religion-state-schools; the audit answers school-vouchers -1 so a merge would conflict, and the position is not a distinct axis.

missingStatements.text: Old Testament civil laws and their penalties should still be applied by governments today.
missingStatements.rationale: This is the core theonomic claim: Frame reports Rushdoony treating almost all Old Testament civil law as literally normative.

notes: Strands differ: Bahnsen held biblical penalties need a Christian culture and cannot be imposed on an unwilling population, and some later writers (McDurmon) dropped the death penalties. Primary-source access was limited to a Chalcedon magazine page; Rushdoony's Institutes was read through Frame's page-cited review.
